title: Count Regression: Workflow
text:
Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(glmmTMB)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)
library(emmeans)
library(broom.mixed)
library(gt)
library(AER)

# 1.3 Data loading
data(NMES1988)
data <- NMES1988

data <- data |>
  select(visits, chronic, health, gender, school, insurance) |>
  mutate(
    health    = fct_relevel(factor(health), "average"),
    gender    = fct_relevel(factor(gender), "male"),
    insurance = fct_relevel(factor(insurance), "no")
  )


Reference groups are average health, male, and no private insurance.





Show code
visits_summary <- data |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(visits),
    variance = var(visits),
    p_zero = mean(visits == 0),
    max = max(visits)
  )

visits_summary |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(mean, variance, p_zero), decimals = 2)








n
mean
variance
p_zero
max




4406
5.77
45.69
0.16
89









Show code
# Create a plot of the overall distribution of the outcome variable (number of visits)
descriptive_plot <- ggplot(data, aes(x = visits)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Number of physician office visits", y = "Number of people")

descriptive_plot









The outcome, the number of physician office visits, is a count: it takes only non-negative whole numbers, and its distribution is strongly right-skewed. Across the 4406 participants, the mean number of visits was 5.77, but the variance was 45.69, about 7.9 times larger than the mean. Because a Poisson model assumes the variance equals the mean, this suggests the data are overdispersed. In addition, 15.5% of participants reported no visits. The maximum was 89 visits, far above the mean (unusually large), indicating a long right tail with a small number of very frequent visitors.

title: Count Regression: Workflow
text:
2. Specifying competing count models

2.1 Why not a Linear Model?


Show code
# Fit a Gaussian model to see why a linear model doesn't work for counts

m_gauss <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = gaussian(link = "identity")
)

#simulation 
set.seed(9041)
res_gauss <- simulateResiduals(m_gauss, n = 500, plot = FALSE)
plot(res_gauss)









The QQ plot is deviating from the diagonal and there is a clear pattern in the residuals across predicted values. It also has deeper problems when applied to counts. It can predict negative numbers of visits, and in this case it predicted a negative count for 1 participant(s). It assumes constant variance, but count variance grows with the mean. In the residual-versus-predicted plot, the quantile lines fan out as predicted values increase, showing that variability grows with the expected count.


2.2 Poisson Models


Show code
# Null (intercept-only) Poisson model: no predictors, just the overall average.
null <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ 1, 
  data = data, 
  family = poisson(link = "log"))

# One-predictor Poisson model: does the number of chronic conditions predict visit counts?
one_pred <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic, 
  data = data, 
  family = poisson(link = "log"))


# Full Poisson model: all five predictors at once.
poisson <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = poisson(link = "log"))




2.3 Exploring my fitted models
Because our models are nested and estimated using the same observations, we can compare all three models in a single anova() call.


Show code
tests <- anova(null, one_pred, poisson)


Each row represents a model. We can retain and rename the statistics relevant to our comparison table.


Show code
tests <- tests |>
  select(Chisq, `Chi Df`, `Pr(>Chisq)`) |>
  rename(
    Nested.df = `Chi Df`,
    Nested.Chisq.stat = Chisq,
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>Chisq)`)


The glance() function from the broom.mixed package returns a one-row data frame containing model-level statistics.
We can apply it to each fitted model.


Show code
glance0 <- broom.mixed::glance(null)
glance1 <- broom.mixed::glance(one_pred)
glance2 <- broom.mixed::glance(poisson)


We can then combine these results using rbind().


Show code
mods <- c(
  "Null",
  "One_Pred: Chronic",
  "Full")

glances <- rbind(
  glance0,
  glance1,
  glance2)


Because the rows in glances and tests represent the same models in the same order, we can combine them using cbind().


Show code
comparison_table <- cbind(
  Model = mods,
  glances,
  tests)




Show code
comparison_table |>
  select(
    Model,
    AIC,
    BIC,
    logLik,
    deviance,
    df.residual,
    Nested.df,
    Nested.Chisq.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    AIC = "AIC",
    BIC = "BIC",
    logLik = "Log-likelihood",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    df.residual = "Residual.df",
    Nested.df = "Nested df",
    Nested.Chisq.stat = "Nested χ²",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      AIC,
      BIC,
      logLik,
      deviance,
      Nested.Chisq.stat
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = Nested.p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        is.na(x),
        "—",
        ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))
      )
    }
  ) |>
  sub_missing(
    columns = c(Nested.df, Nested.Chisq.stat),
    missing_text = "—"
  )

Each row represents one fitted model.
When comparing models, we generally look for lower AIC and BIC values and whether the likelihood-ratio test indicates a statistically significant improvement in model fit.
Remember: The null row has no incremental comparison because it serves as the baseline.


Show code
selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  filter(Nested.p.value < .05) |>
  slice_tail(n = 1)

#creating an object with our selected model's name for dynamic reporting
selected_name <- selected_row$Model

#case matching for dynamic reporting
selected_model <- switch(
  selected_name,
  "Null" = null,
  "One_Pred: Chronic" = one_pred,
  "Full" = poisson)


The provisionally selected model is Full. Adding the number of chronic conditions significantly improved fit over the null model, χ²(1) = 2175.43, p < .001, and adding health, gender, education, and insurance improved fit further, χ²(5) = 959.92, p < .001. The full model also had the lowest AIC and BIC, so it was selected.

title: Count Regression: Workflow
text:
3. Evaluating the Poisson Model

3.1 Simulatin Residuals


Show code
# Set a seed so the simulated residuals are reproducible
set.seed(9041)

# Simulate 500 new datasets from the fitted Poisson model.
res_pois <- simulateResiduals(poisson, n = 500, plot = FALSE)

# Two diagnostic panels: QQ plot (points should follow the diagonal)
# and residuals vs. predicted values (should be flat)
plot(res_pois)











3.2 Testing for overdispersion and excess zeroes


Show code
# Formal dispersion test: is the observed variance bigger (or smaller) than the Poisson model expects?
# A significant p means the variance = mean assumption doesn't hold
disp_pois <- testDispersion(res_pois)









Show code
disp_pois



    DHARMa nonparametric dispersion test via sd of residuals fitted vs.
    simulated

data:  simulationOutput
dispersion = 7.2521, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided




Show code
# Zero-inflation test: does the data have more zeros than the Poisson predicts?
zi_pois <- testZeroInflation(res_pois)









Show code
zi_pois



    DHARMa zero-inflation test via comparison to expected zeros with
    simulation under H0 = fitted model

data:  simulationOutput
ratioObsSim = 15.035, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided




3.3 Interpreting the diagnostics
The DHARMa plots show that the Poisson model fits poorly. The QQ plot deviates strongly from the diagonal, and the residual-versus-predicted plot shows systematic deviations, indicating that the model does not capture how visit counts are distributed.The dispersion ratio is 7.25 (p < .001), and there are 15.03 times as many zeros as the Poisson expects. The observed data are more variable than a Poisson allows.This matters because a Poisson’s standard errors assume variance = mean. When the data are overdispersed, those SEs are too small, CIs are too narrow, and p-values are too optimistic, so predictors may appear significant when they are not. However, the excess zeros should not lead straight to a zero-inflated model because a Poisson model with a mean of about six visits predicts almost no zeros, so the shortage of predicted zeros may simply be another symptom of the overdispersion rather than evidence of a separate process generating zeros.

title: Count Regression: Workflow
section: 4. Fitting and Evaluating a Negative Binomial Model
text:
4. Fitting and Evaluating a Negative Binomial Model

4.1 Estimating the NB2 model
In an effort to address this, a negative binomial model adds a dispersion parameter so the variance can exceed the mean. The Poisson is nested in the NB and we can compare them with a likelihood ratio test (LRT).


Show code
# Negative binomial (NB2) model
neg_binom <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data   = data,
  family = nbinom2(link = "log")
)

summary(neg_binom)


 Family: nbinom2  ( log )
Formula:          visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance
Data: data

      AIC       BIC    logLik -2*log(L)  df.resid 
  24469.9   24521.0  -12227.0   24453.9      4398 


Dispersion parameter for nbinom2 family (): 1.16 

Conditional model:
                 Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)      0.825180   0.058565  14.090  < 2e-16 ***
chronic          0.195759   0.012475  15.692  < 2e-16 ***
healthpoor       0.367664   0.048204   7.627 2.40e-14 ***
healthexcellent -0.373645   0.061542  -6.071 1.27e-09 ***
genderfemale     0.115129   0.031658   3.637 0.000276 ***
school           0.027179   0.004402   6.174 6.67e-10 ***
insuranceyes     0.250155   0.040430   6.187 6.12e-10 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




4.2 Comparing the Poisson and NB2


Show code
# LRT: does the NB fit better than the Poisson?
lrt_nb<-anova(poisson, neg_binom)
lrt_nb


Data: data
Models:
poisson: visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance, zi=~0, disp=~1
neg_binom: visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance, zi=~0, disp=~1
          Df   AIC   BIC logLik deviance Chisq Chi Df Pr(>Chisq)    
poisson    7 36597 36642 -18292    36583                            
neg_binom  8 24470 24521 -12227    24454 12129      1  < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The negative binomial model fit significantly better than the full Poisson model, χ²(1) = 1.212908^{4}, p < .001. The test has one degree of freedom because the NB2 contains exactly one parameter that the Poisson does not: the dispersion parameter (estimated at 1.16), which allows the variance to exceed the mean. This addresses the overdispersion found in Part 3, since the NB2 no longer forces the variance to equal the mean. Whether the NB2 also predicts enough zeros is not answered by this test, so the remaining excess of zeros is checked with DHARMa in 4.3. Switching to the NB2 barely changed the coefficients, but their standard errors became larger; for example, the standard error for chronic conditions grew from 0.004 to 0.012. This shows that the Poisson made the effects look more precise than they really were. All predictors stayed significant, so our main conclusions hold, but with weaker effects the Poisson could have made non-significant predictors look significant.


4.3 Re-checking the NB2 with DHARMa


Show code
# Same seed as before so the residuals are reproducible and comparable to the Poisson check.
set.seed(9041)

# If the NB is adequate, these should now be uniform, unlike the Poisson's.
res_nb <- simulateResiduals(neg_binom, n = 500, plot = FALSE)

# QQ plot: points should now sit close to the diagonal.
# Residuals vs. predicted: should be roughly flat.
plot(res_nb)











Show code
# Dispersion: the ratio should now be close to 1 and non-significant.
disp_nb <- testDispersion(res_nb)









Show code
# Zero inflation: does the NB reproduce the observed number of zeros?
# A non-significant result means the NB's extra variance already accounts for the zeros, so there's no need for a zero-inflated or hurdle model.
zi_nb <- testZeroInflation(res_nb)











4.4 Visualizing the predicted counts


Show code
# Predicted mean visit counts from the additive NB, on the count scale.
# "chronic [0:8]" plots chronic conditions from 0 to 8.
pred_nb <- predict_response(neg_binom, terms = "chronic [0:8]")

plot(pred_nb) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted physician visits by number of chronic conditions",
    x     = "Chronic conditions", y = "Predicted visits"
  )









The line curves upward even though the model is linear in its predictors. That’s the log link: each additional chronic condition adds a constant amount on the log scale, which multiplies the expected count, so the same one-condition increase adds more visits when the expected count is already high.

title: Count Regression: Workflow
section: 5. Deciding whether the zeros need their own model
text:
5. Deciding whether the zeros need their own model

5.1 Making the decision


Show code
# Zero-inflated NB with a constant zero-inflation probability
m_zinb <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ 1,
  data = data, family = nbinom2()
)

# Zero-inflated NB with predictors in the zero part
m_zinb_full <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data, family = nbinom2()
)

# Hurdle NB
m_hurd <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data, family = truncated_nbinom2()
)

# Compare models
lrt_zinb <- anova(neg_binom, m_zinb_full)
lrt_zinb


Data: data
Models:
neg_binom: visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance, zi=~0, disp=~1
m_zinb_full: visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance, zi=~chronic + health + gender + school + insurance, disp=~1
            Df   AIC   BIC logLik deviance  Chisq Chi Df Pr(>Chisq)    
neg_binom    8 24470 24521 -12227    24454                             
m_zinb_full 15 24341 24437 -12155    24311 143.14      7  < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Show code
# The hurdle isn't nested in the NB, so compare with AIC/BIC (lower = better)
aic_tab <- AIC(neg_binom, m_zinb, m_zinb_full, m_hurd)
aic_tab


            df      AIC
neg_binom    8 24469.91
m_zinb       9 24471.19
m_zinb_full 15 24340.77
m_hurd      15 24330.41


Show code
bic_tab <- BIC(neg_binom, m_zinb, m_zinb_full, m_hurd)
bic_tab


            df      BIC
neg_binom    8 24521.03
m_zinb       9 24528.71
m_zinb_full 15 24436.63
m_hurd      15 24426.27


Show code
# Then re-check the chosen model with DHARMa
set.seed(9041)
res_hurd <- simulateResiduals(m_hurd, n = 500, plot = FALSE)
plot(res_hurd)









Show code
zi_hurd <- testZeroInflation(res_hurd)









Show code
zi_hurd



    DHARMa zero-inflation test via comparison to expected zeros with
    simulation under H0 = fitted model

data:  simulationOutput
ratioObsSim = 0.99928, p-value = 1
alternative hypothesis: two.sided




5.2 Justifying my choice
Because the NB2 still predicted too few zeros, we fit a zero-inflated NB and a hurdle NB. The zero-inflated NB fit significantly better than the NB2, χ²(7) = 143.14, p < .001, which shows that the zeros needed their own model. The hurdle NB had the lowest AIC and BIC of all the models, and its DHARMa zero-inflation test was not significant (ratio = 1, p = 1), meaning it predicts the right number of zeros. I therefore chose the hurdle NB, which treats whether someone visits a physician at all separately from how often they visit.

title: Count Regression: Workflow
text:
6. Testing and Probing an Interaction

6.1 My Prediction
I expected private insurance to moderate the relationship between chronic conditions and physician visits. Insured people with more chronic conditions should be better able to act on their extra health needs. The slope of chronic conditions should therefore be steeper for insured than for uninsured people.


6.2 Fitting the Interaction Model


Show code
# Hurdle NB model with a chronic x insurance interaction in both parts.
# chronic * insurance expands to chronic + insurance + chronic:insurance, so both main effects and the product term are included automatically.
# The other predictors (health, gender, school) are controls.
interact <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ health + gender + school + chronic * insurance,
  ziformula = ~ health + gender + school + chronic * insurance,
  data   = data,
  family = truncated_nbinom2()
)

summary(interact)


 Family: truncated_nbinom2  ( log )
Formula:          visits ~ health + gender + school + chronic * insurance
Zero inflation:          ~health + gender + school + chronic * insurance
Data: data

      AIC       BIC    logLik -2*log(L)  df.resid 
  24333.9   24442.6  -12150.0   24299.9      4389

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




6.3 Testing whether the interaction is needed


Show code
# LRT: does adding the chronic x insurance interaction improve fit over the additive hurdle model?
lrt_int <- anova(m_hurd, interact)
lrt_int


Data: data
Models:
m_hurd: visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance, zi=~chronic + health + gender + school + insurance, disp=~1
interact: visits ~ health + gender + school + chronic * insurance, zi=~health + gender + school + chronic * insurance, disp=~1
         Df   AIC   BIC logLik deviance  Chisq Chi Df Pr(>Chisq)
m_hurd   15 24330 24426 -12150    24300                         
interact 17 24334 24443 -12150    24300 0.4639      2      0.793


Adding the chronic × insurance interaction did not significantly improve fit over the additive hurdle model, χ²(2) = 0.46, p = 0.793. The test has two degrees of freedom because the interaction was added to both parts of the hurdle model. We probe the interaction below anyway. The omnibus test only tells us whether the slopes differ overall, while probing shows what the association actually looks like within each insurance group and how large the insurance difference is at different numbers of chronic conditions.


6.4 Plotting predicted points


Show code
# Predicted mean visit counts from the interaction model, on the count scale.
pred_int <- predict_response(interact, terms = c("chronic", "insurance"))

plot(pred_int) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(no = "green4", yes = "peachpuff")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(no = "green4", yes = "peachpuff")) +
  labs(
    title  = "Predicted physician visits by chronic conditions and insurance",
    x      = "Chronic conditions", y = "Predicted visits",
    colour = NULL, fill = NULL
  )











6.5 Probing the interaction


Show code
# Simple slopes: the slope of chronic estimated separately within each insurance group (count part).
slopes <- emtrends(
  interact, 
  specs = ~ insurance, 
  var = "chronic",
  component = "cond")

pairs(slopes)


 contrast estimate     SE  df z.ratio p.value
 no - yes   0.0164 0.0282 Inf   0.583  0.5598

Results are averaged over the levels of: health, gender 


Show code
#test simple slopes against zero
slopes_sum <- summary(slopes, infer = TRUE)
slopes_sum


 insurance chronic.trend     SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL z.ratio p.value
 no                0.160 0.0247 Inf     0.111     0.208   6.462 <0.0001
 yes               0.143 0.0144 Inf     0.115     0.172   9.945 <0.0001

Results are averaged over the levels of: health, gender 
Confidence level used: 0.95 




Show code
# Pick the probing values: low (-1 SD), average (mean) and high (+1 SD) chronic conditions.
chronic_mean <- mean(data$chronic, na.rm = TRUE)
chronic_sd <- sd(data$chronic, na.rm = TRUE)
chronic_values <- chronic_mean + c(-1, 0, 1) * chronic_sd

# Estimated marginal means (EMMs) for each insurance group at each chronic value.
ins_emmeans <- emmeans(
  interact,
  specs = ~ insurance | chronic,
  at = list(chronic = chronic_values),
  component = "cond"
)

# Estimated mean visit counts in each insurance x chronic cell.
summary(ins_emmeans, type = "response")

For the simple slopes: The pairs(slopes) test reproduces the count-part interaction coefficient from summary(interact), with the same standard error and p-value but with the sign flipped, because pairs computes No - Yes, whereas the coefficient compares Yes with No. With a binary moderator, “do the two slopes differ?” is the question the product term answers, so the two tests are the same test.
For the simple effects: Why don’t these counts match the plot exactly? ggeffects holds health and gender at their reference levels (average, male), while emmeans averages over their levels. The insurance contrasts are the same either way, because with no interaction involving health or gender their effects cancel out of the comparison.

6.7 Interpreting the Interaction
There is no evidence that the association between chronic conditions and physician visits differs by insurance status. Adding the interaction did not improve fit, χ²(2) = 0.46, p = 0.793, and the simple slopes of chronic conditions were positive and very similar for people with and without private insurance. The simple effects also showed that insured people visited the physician more often at every level of chronic conditions, with a gap that stayed about the same size. Because the omnibus test and the probing results agree, I am fairly confident that insurance does not change how chronic conditions relate to visits, although insurance on its own is still associated with more visits.

title: Count Regression: Workflow
text:
7. Write-up and Discussion

7.1 Results write-up
Physician office visits were overdispersed (M = 5.77, s² = 45.69; 16% zeros). A Poisson model showed significant overdispersion (dispersion ratio = 7.25, p < .001) and excess zeros (observed/expected = 15.03, p < .001). A negative binomial model fit significantly better, χ²(1) = 1.212908^{4}, p < .001, and resolved the overdispersion (ratio = 1.04, p = 0.432), but still underpredicted the zeros (ratio = 1.1, p < .001). A hurdle negative binomial model had the lowest AIC and BIC and reproduced the zeros (ratio = 1), so it was selected.
Holding other predictors constant, among people who visited a physician, more chronic conditions (b = 0.15, 95% CI [0.12, 0.17], p < .001), poor rather than average health (b = 0.38, 95% CI [0.29, 0.48], p < .001), more education (b = 0.02, 95% CI [0.01, 0.03], p < .001), and private insurance (b = 0.13, 95% CI [0.05, 0.22], p = 0.003) were associated with more visits, while excellent health was associated with fewer (b = -0.37, 95% CI [-0.5, -0.24], p < .001). Gender was not significant (b = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.12], p = 0.088). In the zero part, people with more chronic conditions, women, people with more education, and insured people were less likely to have no visits, people in excellent health were more likely to have none, and poor health did not predict whether people visited at all.
Adding a chronic conditions × insurance interaction did not improve fit, χ²(2) = 0.46, p = 0.793. Chronic conditions were associated with more visits both without private insurance (b = 0.16, 95% CI [0.11, 0.21]) and with it (b = 0.14, 95% CI [0.12, 0.17]), both p < .001. Uninsured people made fewer visits than insured people at −1 SD (b = -0.16, p = 0.014), the mean (b = -0.14, p = 0.002), and +1 SD (b = -0.11, p = 0.028) of chronic conditions, so the insurance gap stayed about the same regardless of how many chronic conditions people had.


7.2 Discussion
Chronic conditions were the most important predictor of physician visits. People with more conditions were more likely to visit at all and visited more often. Self-perceived health was the next most important, with poor health linked to more visits and excellent health to fewer. Insurance, education and gender played smaller roles, suggesting that health need matters more than access or individual differences. The main limitations are that the data are observational, so the results are correlation not causation. Visits and health were self-reported which is not the most reliable and the data come from older Americans in 1987–1988, so the findings may not apply to other groups or to today’s health-care system.
